sg.name: Lina El-Jawhari
paragraphs: “Better to die standing than to live on your knees.” - Ernesto Che Guevara. As an Arab, living on my knees was not an option to begin with, for if I knelt for a second, I would be trampled on, silenced, and buried.

Growing up in Amman, I did not face discrimination as an Arab, so I was blissfully unaware of the true struggle that came with the race. As I grew older, I watched my siblings become more versed in the world of politics, and so I followed suit. Through that, I discovered how deep-rooted the discrimination really was. Even when Western media tries to sugar-coat it, we are still more susceptible to the “random” searches at the airport, stabbings in London and not receiving call-backs from potential work opportunities due to Arab names. As I saw all of this first-hand, I knew I had to do something, I just did not know what.

I was a meek child, shying away often from simple social interactions, but then, a formative experience occurred, my eldest sister joined MUN. From there, a chain reaction happened, and the outcome was me joining Model United Nations. For that, I am beholden to my sibling. MUN helped me find my voice; I had a lot of the information, but I learned to stand up and speak.

That was not all I obtained from MUN, as I gained new friendships, I procured the ability to see from eyes that were not my own. I learned how the same statement can be interpreted a thousand different ways. I grasped the concept that however much I think I know, I know nothing. With that realisation, I researched more, and with that research, I uncovered how much injustice was all around, not just for Arabs, for everyone.

Naturally, I was frustrated and overwhelmed. Once those feelings subsided, all that was left was hope. Nonetheless, hope alone is not enough, resilience and persistence must follow. We can make a difference through everything we do, from donating change to a charity, to spreading awareness, to debates and even starting an organization. The change starts with us. We are the ones that must act, and we must do so together. One voice can be heard, but multiple voices cannot be ignored. This is how we can Turn the Tide.
Welcome to AsriyyaMUN’27, and it is my honor to serve as the Secretary General this year.

hoc.name: Jeeda AbuKhalaf
paragraphs: Growing up in a region where political tensions are ever-present, I was steeped in the fire of political awareness. A flame that didn’t just light my path, but shaped my purpose. This made me believe in the importance of using my voice to advocate for others. And my mission was clear; to turn vision into voice, and voice into change.

Rather than watching conflicts from afar, I found a way to turn thought and curiosity into action. I became interested in understanding how the world works and that opened my eyes to the fact that this process isn't easy. It taught me that the first and most important step of it all is knowing the power and value of words. This is where I found Model United Nations, it proved that the brilliant mind of the youth does in fact rule. I was extremely thrilled to see the procedure of two sides looking at the same political issue yet speaking about it from two different angles. Following the discussions where they work on bringing both views together never failed to fascinate me.
“The youth of today are the leaders of tomorrow.” — Nelson Mandela

As young leaders, WE are the foundation of the future, WE are the catalyst for change and WE have the power to create a better tomorrow. Young brilliant minds have the power to shape a world that is not daunting but exciting, full of opportunities rather than aggression. That is why we, the AsriyyaMUN’27 team, have worked wholeheartedly to infuse our core values into this conference.

theme.title: Turn The Tide
paragraphs: With the rise in popularity of social media and the increased accessibility of information, most people are glaringly aware of the current economic and political state of the world and the fact that it is in a phase of complete disorder. Moreover, the more information we obtain, the more we realize we know nothing. The number of catastrophes that are occurring simultaneously, smothers anything resembling good news, and that makes it increasingly difficult to be hopeful. The loss of that hope is disastrous, as without hope, without seeing the light at the end of the tunnel, the effort to fix the world fizzles out. This loss of motivation is also caused by the overwhelming number of communities in shambles all around; from genocides, to poverty, to child marriage and many other issues, it is almost expected at this point to turn a blind eye and conform into an inactive member of society, not fixing anything, not contributing either. But is that actually being inactive?

Doing nothing is doing something; by deliberately ignoring these problems, we are complicit. So, what does one do in this situation? We cannot fix everything at once, and the news just keeps coming in waves. We must Turn the Tide, which is the theme for AsriyyaMUN’27. What that means is: we must use the momentum carried by these disasters to our advantage; use the outrage, the anger, the exposure to change the outcome, because right now, if things continue in the direction they are moving towards, the world is in for more struggling and greater decline. By trying to tackle one issue at a time, we can gradually change the direction these waves are going in; we can secure better futures and better lives for the whole world. Things have reached an extreme, and turning the tide reverses the course of events, from one extreme, to another.
